articles.title: Abelhas em São José dos Campos: enxames em telhado e caçamba | G1
articles.standfirst: Abelhas mudaram de lugar após moradores mexerem em um enxame no telhado e se concentraram em uma caçamba, segundo comerciante; biólogo explica o comportamento e orienta como prevenir novos enxames.
articles.summary: Enxames de abelhas em São José dos Campos invadem imóveis após serem perturbados, e biólogo orienta sobre os riscos e a forma correta de remoção dos insetos.
articles.body:
Dois enxames de abelhas na Rua Virgem, em São José dos Campos , no interior de São Paulo, têm causado preocupação em quem mora ou passa pela via do Jardim Satélite.

Segundo o comerciante Wanderson Vilela, o problema começou no sábado (17), quando as abelhas estavam concentradas em um cacho na ponta do telhado de um imóvel. Após alguém mexer no local, os insetos começaram a sobrevoar a rua e a mudar de lugar, até se concentrarem também na caçamba.

“Quando elas levantam voo, fazem uma nuvem na rua. Agora, no anoitecer, elas vão começar a voar e buscar onde tem iluminação. [...] Elas vêm bater em uma lâmpada fluorescente e entram dentro do escritório, das casas”, relatou Wanderson Vilela.

Wanderson afirma que acionou a Prefeitura de São José dos Campos e o Corpo de Bombeiros para pedir ajuda. Segundo o comerciante, os bombeiros chegaram a fazer um isolamento no local.

Procurada, a Prefeitura de São José dos Campos informou na tarde desta segunda-feira (19) que acionará a equipe responsável para atender a solicitação no local.

"[A Prefeitura] esclarece ainda que, quando se trata de uma área particular, a responsabilidade pela avaliação e contratação de um especialista é do proprietário. Neste caso, como a ocorrência das abelhas está situada agora em uma área pública, uma equipe técnica será enviada ao local", disse, em nota.

Um biólogo ouvido pelo g1 explicou que a divisão do enxame pode estar ligada à reprodução e orientou como prevenir a instalação de abelhas em imóveis (leia mais abaixo).

Enxame de abelhas em caçamba preocupa moradores em São José dos Campos. — Foto: Wanderson Vilela

Divisão dos enxames pode estar relacionada à reprodução

A divisão do enxame pode fazer parte do ciclo reprodutivo natural das abelhas, segundo o biólogo Davi Nunes Veloso. Nesse processo, parte das abelhas acompanha uma nova rainha para formar outra colônia.

O especialista explica que a interferência humana pode ter influenciado o comportamento dos insetos ou antecipado essa divisão. Ele também alerta que, aparentemente, as abelhas podem ser africanizadas, conhecidas pelo comportamento defensivo. A identificação, porém, não foi confirmada.

Segundo Veloso, a primavera e o verão são períodos favoráveis à reprodução desses animais, e as temperaturas mais altas podem acelerar esse processo.

O biólogo Davi Nunes Veloso orienta que, como prevenção, frestas e buracos em telhados que possam servir de abrigo para os animais sejam vedados. No caso de enxames já instalados, ele recomenda procurar um profissional que trabalhe com apicultura para avaliar a retirada com equipamentos de proteção adequados.

Segundo o especialista, uma das possibilidades é retirar a abelha rainha, fazendo com que o restante do enxame a acompanhe. O procedimento, porém, exige conhecimento técnico e equipamentos específicos, já que as abelhas podem reagir à aproximação.

articles.title: Elon Musk promises to give one SpaceX share to every child in the US
articles.summary: Elon Musk says he plans to give one of his SpaceX shares to every child in the US, amounting to around $10.5 billion worth of shares.
articles.body: Elon Musk says he plans to give one of his SpaceX shares to every child in the US starting next year. With around 72 million children in the US as of July 2025, Musk would be giving away about $10.5 billion worth of shares, according to a report from CNBC. Musk, who runs SpaceX and Tesla, appears to be giving away the shares through Trump Accounts, the tax-advantaged investment accounts for American children. Musk responded to a post from Brad Gerstner, who helped launch Trump Accounts, saying “Thanks for helping enable this.” Musk adds that this giveaway “will be the first of many.” The move comes just months after SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell announced that she’d be giving shares of her SpaceX stock to 2 million Trump Accounts. Dell’s founder similarly poured $6.25 billion into Trump Accounts, while Micron also announced a $250 million investment. Along with giving away SpaceX shares, Musk has made large contributions to Republican midterm election efforts. Musk donated $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund PAC in September, making up more than “half of the super PAC’s total receipts in the third quarter of this year,” according to CBS News. He also dumped $76 million into the Super PAC he founded in 2024, America PAC. Update, October 19th: Added context from Musk.

articles.title: Amelia Earhart search suffers crushing setback after researchers make disappointing find
articles.summary: Purdue University revealed the Nikumaroro lagoon anomaly suspected to be Amelia Earhart's missing plane was actually tree debris with a carbonate coating.
articles.body: Researchers who embarked on a grueling journey to find Amelia Earhart's missing plane have suffered a devastating setback. Purdue University announced that the team had "found no conclusive evidence" to confirm the Taraia Object hypothesis — which suggested that wreckage from Earhart's aircraft lay in a lagoon on the remote Pacific island of Nikumaroro. The theory centered on the Taraia Object, a visual anomaly first spotted in satellite imagery in 2020 that researchers suspected could be wreckage of Earhart's Lockheed Electra 10-E. ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER UNEXPECTED TWIST IN SHIPWRECK MYSTERY AFTER CLUES DON'T ADD UP But the university said the object was "likely a collection of large trees deposited along the peninsula’s sandspit." The university added, "By the time the team arrived at the site, a good portion of the debris had fragmented and washed away, leaving only a single Y-shaped segment — a fraction of the anomaly’s original size observed in imagery when the Taraia Object hypothesis was developed." The remaining fragment's reflective surface was caused by a "carbonate veneer," which researchers said had made the debris appear metallic. "Other items found by the team were similarly coated with a shiny concretized amalgam of coral sand," the university added. HAUNTING CLUES EMERGE IN 7-YEAR FISHING BOAT MYSTERY AFTER WRECKAGE FOUND OFF ISLAND Despite the setback, Rick Pettigrew, executive director of the Archaeological Legacy Institute (ALI) and leader of the expedition, said the team "remains in great spirits and proud of what was accomplished." "We accomplished our goal to determine what the Taraia Object was, and we’re deeply grateful to the private donors who shared our vision and made this journey possible," he said in a statement. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Officials added that the expedition uncovered several artifacts, including a 30-inch steel tube, that could offer clues about how debris travels through the island's lagoon and accumulates along the Taraia Peninsula. The discoveries will undergo further study, though officials did not report finding any artifacts conclusively linked to Earhart's missing aircraft. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Despite the disappointing development, researchers aren't giving up on the theory that Earhart ended up on Nikumaroro. "While the expedition did not uncover the 'smoking gun' connecting Earhart to Nikumaroro, the team reiterated its collective belief in the broader castaway hypothesis," Purdue University added. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Earhart vanished on July 2, 1937, while attempting to become the first woman to fly around the world. The famed aviator and her navigator, Fred Noonan, disappeared while flying from Lae, New Guinea, to Howland Island during one of the final stretches of their journey. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Earhart was just 39 years old when she vanished, leaving behind one of aviation history's most enduring unsolved mysteries.

articles.title: Amazon is funding a new nuclear plant in Indiana
articles.summary: Amazon has signed an agreement with X-energy and American Electric Power (AEP) to fund the building of a new nuclear energy facility in Indiana.
articles.body: Amazon has signed an agreement with X-energy and American Electric Power (AEP) to fund the building of a new nuclear energy facility in Indiana. The proposed plant, which would replace the now defunct coal-fueled Breed Generating Station in Fairbanks, Sullivan County, aims to provide up to 960 megawatts of carbon-free energy for both the regional power grid and Amazon’s data centers. No timeline for construction or operation has been announced for the facility, which Amazon says “could” create 1,000 construction jobs and 100 permanent roles. The facility in Indiana is targeting to build 12 Xe-100 SMR’s, an advanced (but unproven) reactor that’s still undergoing development and licensing. These reactors can be cooled using either air, water, or a hybrid solution of both, which Amazon says should allow them to be deployed in water-constrained regions without impacting water demand in local communities. Indiana also happens to be home to a famously expensive and uncompleted energy project called the Marble Hill Nuclear Power Plant. It was abandoned half-finished in 1983 after $2.5 billion had already been sunk into it, and has been under continued demolition since 2008. Terms for Amazon’s agreement in Fairbanks haven’t been disclosed, so we can’t compare the cost between the facilities. This marks the second nuclear energy project that Amazon and X-energy are collaborating on, with the collective goal of working with regional utilities to deploy more than 5 gigawatts of new nuclear capacity in the US by 2039. In October last year, Amazon shared an early preview of its first planned nuclear plant, the Cascade Advanced Energy Facility in Washington. That project is similarly set to build 12 advanced reactors and create local jobs, but construction isn’t expected to start until the end of this decade. Amazon is one of several tech companies, including Meta, Microsoft, and Google, that are exploring their own nuclear energy projects to power AI data centers. Investing in energy grid infrastructure was also one of the commitments that Amazon outlined in a lengthy blog post earlier this month that aimed to sway some of the growing negativity around data center projects, though it’ll be many years before anyone — including Amazon — can reap the benefits of these new facilities.

articles.title: Amazon to fund 12 small nuclear reactors at former Indiana coal plant | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Amazon and X-energy have inked another deal to deploy nuclear power to the grid. This one will generate nearly 1 gigawatt of electricity.
articles.body:
Amazon is funding development of a proposed 960-megawatt nuclear plant in Indiana and would be the first customer to buy its power, the companies announced Monday. Utility company American Electric Power (AEP) would operate the plant. X-energy, which designs small modular nuclear reactors and went public in April, would supply the reactors.

The new power plant would consist of 12 Xe-100 small modular reactors and be located on the site of a demolished coal power plant just south of Terre Haute. The deal is the second commercial agreement between Amazon and X-energy, and it’s three times larger than the first , which was announced two years ago.

Amazon has invested heavily in X-energy, leading a $700 million Series C-1 round in October 2024. The two companies have said they ultimately plan to build 5 gigawatts of new nuclear generating capacity in the U.S. by 2039.

Unlike many newly announced power plants, these reactors would be connected to the public electric grid, though Amazon says the power would also serve its data centers.

The companies’ aggressive timeline still depends on X-energy successfully delivering its first power plant at a Dow Chemical plant southeast of Houston, Texas. The site, called Seadrift, has recently been at the center of a lawsuit filed by the state of Texas, which accuses the plant of “habitual non-compliance” with water and solid-waste regulations and permits.

X-energy has yet to break ground at Seadrift, which will host four Xe-100 reactors to provide the chemical plant with heat and electricity. The company said its construction permit is in the final phases of the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission’s review process.

Startups and large cloud computing companies are betting that small modular reactors (SMRs), like the kind being developed by X-energy, will help pull the nuclear industry out of its slump. The most recent nuclear power plants built in the U.S. suffered from egregious budget overruns and slipped timelines.

By shrinking the reactor, companies like X-energy hope that mass manufacturing will costs and schedules in line. Even then, it could be a tall order. Experts say mass manufacturing often doesn’t start producing benefits for about a decade .

X-energy debuted on the Nasdaq in April in an IPO priced at $23 per share. Investor excitement drove the price up 27% in the first day of trading, but shares of the newly public company have dropped by nearly two-thirds since then.

News of the Amazon deal sent X-energy’s shares up about 10% in pre-market trading, though they were down by less than 2% at the time of publication.

articles.title: Search for Amelia Earhart answers isn't over. Here's what's next
articles.summary: After an expedition for Amelia Earhart's plane came up empty, attention has turned to other searches and theories related to her disappearance.
articles.body:
Satellite images taken a decade ago captured a plane-like shape on a remote island, fueling theories that it could be the wreckage of the aircraft flown by pioneering aviator Amelia Earhart when she disappeared in 1937 during her ambitious round-the-world flight.

The photographs led to a highly anticipated October expedition that Purdue University described as the best chance yet at locating the vanished aircraft. Enthusiasts around the globe watched with bated breath , hoping the nearly 90-year mystery would be solved.

But on Oct. 19, the expedition team announced that the object was not Earhart's Electra 10E plane , but rather likely a "collection of large trees."

Amelia Earhart expedition investigates new clues. See the mission

"We accomplished our goal to determine what the Taraia Object was, and we're deeply grateful to the private donors who shared our vision and made this journey possible," lead archaeologist Rick Pettigrew said in a statement. "Our team remains in great spirits and proud of what was accomplished."

The latest expedition follows the same pattern as every other that came before it – great anticipation followed by dashed hopes and disappointment. Two years ago, an exploration company announced that what it thought was Earhart's plane on the ocean floor was just a rock formation .

But despite the many failed attempts to find out what happened to the trailblazing pilot, researchers and expedition companies don't appear to be slowing down their efforts to locate the missing aircraft. Deep sea exploration company Nauticos is raising money for its fourth search for Earhart's plane.

"It's the greatest unsolved mystery of the 20th century," said Dorothy Cochrane, a retired general aviation curator at the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum and a leading expert on Amelia Earhart. "She was a worldwide celebrity and what happened leaves people unfulfilled. I don't anticipate the interest going away."

New search for Amelia Earhart underway. See her record-breaking career

News of the expedition, which was a joint effort between Purdue University, the Purdue Research Foundation and the Archaeological Legacy Institute, drew international headlines as researchers appeared to be on the cusp of a major finding.

"I am feeling very confident about this," Pettigrew told USA TODAY ahead of the expedition . "I'm pumped."

In early October, a 17-person team journeyed by plane and boat to Nikumaroro, a small Pacific island between Australia and Hawaii, where a popular theory suggested Earhart and Noonan may have landed there during their ill-fated attempt to circumnavigate the globe.

The theory is largely based on images of the "Taraia Object," a visual anomaly in the island's lagoon identified through satellite imagery that some believed to be Earhart's plane.

But after several days on the island, the team announced that it found no conclusive evidence linking the object to Earhart's aircraft. Researchers determined that the visual anomaly was likely a collection of large trees and other debris deposited along a sandspit on the island.

"By the time the team arrived at the site, a good portion of the debris had fragmented and washed away, leaving only a single Y-shaped segment — a fraction of the anomaly's original size observed in imagery when the Taraia Object hypothesis was developed," Purdue University said in a news release .

Earhart's disappearance remains a subject of fierce debate

The expedition is among dozens of costly voyages that have taken researchers from remote islands to the depths of the Pacific Ocean in hopes of finding Earhart's Lockheed Electra 10E.

Several of the expeditions are based on different theories surrounding Earhart's unsolved disappearance. The most widely accepted explanation is that Earhart and Noonan ran out of fuel and crashed into the Pacific Ocean near Howland Island, where the pair were expected to land before they vanished.

Some of the more implausible theories suggest the flight was part of a secret spy mission, that Earhart assumed another identity or that Earhart and Noonan were captured by a foreign government.

Amelia Earhart images revisit her life as new search planned

In a statement, Purdue said the research team supports the broader "castaway theory," which posits that Earhart and Noonan did not crash into the sea, but rather landed on the reef flat of Nikumaroro and were marooned there.

During the recent expedition, the team located several artifacts that they intend to study, including a steel tube about 30 inches long, according to Purdue. These items could be the latest pieces of evidence supporting the theory that Earhart and Noonan landed on Nikumaroro, the university said, including radio bearings that converge there, and an analysis of human bones discovered on the island which resemble a person of Earhart's stature.

With the decades-old mystery remaining unsolved, other researchers and exploration companies are poised to move ahead with their own searches.

Last year, deep sea exploration company Nauticos announced plans for a fourth expedition . In a statement, the company said it will search an area near Howland Island where an analysis suggests Earhart and Noonan were located less than an hour before their last radio transmissions.

"We have narrowed the search area dramatically," Dave Jourdan, President of Nauticos, said in a statement. "This new expedition presents our best chance yet to finally locate Amelia Earhart's plane."

Purdue University, where Earhart worked as a visiting professor, said it remains committed to solving the enduring mystery. It has not announced plans for any future expeditions.

"Amelia Earhart never gave up — she kept pushing boundaries and flying into the unknown," Steve Schultz, Purdue general counsel and a member of the recent expedition, said in a statement. "That same fire fuels our search. She kept flying, and we will keep searching."

Christopher Cann is a national reporter for USA TODAY. He can be reached by email at ccann@usatoday.com.

articles.title: Watch: Japan launches historic Mars mission to probe mysterious moons, bring samples back
articles.summary: Japan launched a spacecraft towards Mars on Tuesday on a historic five-year mission to explore the Red Planet’s mysterious moons, Phobos and Deimos, and
articles.body: Japan launched a spacecraft towards Mars on Tuesday on a historic five-year mission to explore the Red Planet’s mysterious moons, Phobos and Deimos, and bring back samples to Earth. Led by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), the mission aims to collect at least 10 grams of material from Phobos, marking the first attempt to retrieve samples from the Martian sphere.The spacecraft lifted off before dawn from Tanegashima Island, Japan’s main spaceport, as five space agencies joined forces for the ambitious project. If successful, the mission, known as Martian Moons Exploration (MMX), will deliver dust, soil and rock samples from Phobos to Earth in 2031, potentially offering new insights into the origins of Mars’ moons and the evolution of the Solar System.Despite decades of Mars exploration, no spacecraft has ever landed on either Phobos or Deimos, the planet’s two small moons. While the United States and China have successfully landed spacecraft on Mars, retrieving samples from the planet or its moons remains an unaccomplished feat. Japan, however, enters the mission with experience from two successful asteroid sample-return missions.Why Japan is targeting Mars’ moonsThe $578 million mission will investigate how Phobos and Deimos formed, addressing a long-standing debate in planetary science. One theory suggests the moons emerged from debris scattered into orbit after a massive object collided with Mars. Another proposes that they are asteroids captured by the planet’s gravitational pull.Phobos, the larger and closer of the two moons, is an irregular, potato-shaped object measuring about 22 kilometres across. Scientists believe its surface material could preserve clues about the early history of the Martian system and the processes that shaped the planet.By studying samples collected from Phobos alongside observations of Deimos and Mars, researchers hope to understand how planetary bodies formed and how materials such as water and organic compounds were transported across the Solar System. The mission will also examine Mars’ atmosphere and the surrounding space environment to investigate how atmospheric material escapes into space.Rover deployment and sample returnThe five-tonne MMX spacecraft is expected to reach the Martian system in late summer 2027. It will study the two moons before deploying a French-German rover, named Idefix after the white terrier in the Asterix comics, to the surface of Phobos.The spacecraft will then attempt to collect at least 10 grams of surface material before beginning its return journey to Earth. The mission is expected to last approximately five years, with the samples scheduled to arrive in 2031.Beyond its scientific objectives, MMX will test technologies needed for future exploration of Mars, including landing operations on small celestial bodies, advanced sampling systems and long-distance communications. With communication delays of up to 44 minutes for a round trip, the spacecraft must operate with considerable autonomy.

articles.title: The fossil fuel comeback is here
articles.summary: Plans for new gas plants have spiked while renewable energy projects face cancellations, even as AI data centers drive up electricity demand.
articles.body: The US is building more fossil fuel infrastructure than it has in a decade while renewable energy growth slows down, a new report shows. Electricity demand is also climbing faster than it has in more than a decade with more data centers, factories, and electric vehicles plugging into the grid. Despite those growing demands, the Trump administration has sought to hobble the wind and solar industries in favor of fossil fuels. America’s energy landscape is already shifting as a result, according to the report published last week by the nonprofit Environmental Defense Fund and research firm Atlas Public Policy. If all the gas projects in the development pipeline complete construction, they could lock in more pollution and higher electricity prices for decades, the authors warn. “The U.S. power sector is at a new inflection point, with decisions made today shaping the cost, reliability, and emissions profile of the grid for decades to come,” the report says. While the US still generates 60 percent of its electricity from fossil fuels, renewables have quickly gained ground. Wind and solar produced more electricity together than coal for the first time in 2024. Solar was the fastest-growing source of new electricity generation that year, accounting for 81 percent of added capacity. Globally, solar has become the cheapest power source in most of the world. Then Donald Trump stepped into his second term as president with a plan to “drill, baby, drill” for fossil fuels, his preferred power source for energy-hungry data centers. His administration has sought to kill renewable energy projects by issuing stop work orders, blocking permits, and removing tax incentives. We’re still seeing a rush of new solar and wind farms driven by relatively low costs, although many of them make up the last wave of projects that benefited from Biden-era incentives. The winds are shifting in favor of gas-fired power plants. Plans for new fossil fuel infrastructure climbed from just 5 percent of all new capacity in 2024 to 30 percent by the second quarter of 2026, according to the new report, which analyzes data from the US Energy Information Administration. If the trend continues, fossil fuels could make up 70 percent of the development pipeline by the end of the decade. Planned fossil capacity would reach 68 gigawatts by 2030, reflecting a 45 percent jump from construction plans just six months ago. Many of those plans could still fall through, particularly if forecasts for AI data center energy demand are overblown. But for now, renewable energy projects are being canceled at a faster clip than fossil fuels, at 4.9 percent compared to 2.9 percent of projects, respectively. New utility-scale solar and wind farms still beat gas when it comes to cost, coming in at $68 to $69 per megawatt-hour on average compared to $90 per megawatt-hour for new combined-cycle natural gas plants, the report finds. Fossil fuels are also subject to increasing price volatility, particularly since the US instigated war with Iran. Gas and coal power plants also emit air pollutants and the greenhouse gases causing climate change, leading to more health costs. Electricity bills have risen across the nation as utilities upgrade power grids and build new energy infrastructure to meet rising demand.

articles.title: Aerobics can help fight memory loss induced by sleep deprivation: Study
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Forgotten where you put your keys, struggled to recall something you just read or found it harder to absorb new information after a sleepless
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Forgotten where you put your keys, struggled to recall something you just read or found it harder to absorb new information after a sleepless night? There may be reason for that. Sleep deprivation can make it harder for the brain to form new memories. But a brief bout of exercise may help counter some of that damage, a new study suggests.Researchers found that 20 minutes of aerobic exercise helped preserve the ability to form new memories even after 30 hours without sleep. A 90-minute nap offered a comparable benefit, with both groups performing around 22% better on a memory task than participants who received no intervention.Published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the study involved 53 healthy adults aged 18 to 35 who were kept awake for 30 hours under laboratory monitoring. They were divided into three groups - 18 did 20 minutes of aerobic exercise, 18 took a 90-minute nap and 17 sat on an exercise bike for 20 minutes without exercising as the control group. When tested on image recognition three days later, the exercise group correctly recognised 56% of the images, the nap group 57% and the control group 46%. Difference between the exercise and nap groups was not statistically significant.Electroencephalography (EEG) recordings suggested that the two interventions supported memory through different neural mechanisms. In the nap group, changes linked to reduced sleep pressure and neural fatigue helped explain performance, while in the exercise group, how the brain processed incoming information was more closely linked to successful memory formation. The findings may be relevant to people in sleep-deprived professions, including healthcare, though the study did not establish benefits in real-world settings.Prof Manjari Tripathi, head of neurology at AIIMS, said deep non-REM sleep helps consolidate episodic memories, while REM (rapid eye movement) sleep supports emotional memory processing. Repeated sleep deprivation can cause brain fog, fatigue, poor memory and emotional outbursts, and may raise depression risk. Short naps of around 15 minutes may help night-shift workers, but cannot replace seven-eight hours of consolidated sleep.Dr JC Suri, director and head of pulmonary, critical care and sleep medicine at Sitaram Bhartia Institute of Science and Research, said the findings showed a "genuine but narrow protective effect" on episodic memory after acute sleep deprivation.Since the study involved acute sleep deprivation in healthy young adults, further research is needed to establish whether the benefits extend to chronic sleep insufficiency or real-world settings.

articles.title: Marine life dramatically declined in Gulf of Mexico in years after BP oil spill, study finds
articles.summary: After BP’s 2010 Deepwater Horizon explosion and the ensuing oil spill, the number of marine animals in part of the Gulf of Mexico plummeted, a new study found.
articles.body: In a deep, dark part of the Gulf of Mexico, the number of marine animals plummeted by about 60% in the years following the 2010 Deepwater Horizon explosion, a new study found. In a crucial part of the Gulf between the light surface and the darkest depths, where the BP-operated well failed and dumped 134 million gallons of oil, the number of fish found dropped by 63.5% from the year after the spill to 2015. Crustaceans, including shrimp and krill, a key food for whales, went down 62%, and larger animals like squid and octopuses fell 59.7%, according to a study published Monday in the journal PNAS. And those populations haven’t come close to recovering, the study found. Researchers focused on the ocean's “twilight zone,” a vast area above the seafloor, where much of the surface marine life, including dolphins and whales, feast on creatures. Yet little is known about this gigantic ecosystem, and this region of the Gulf had not been studied before the 2010 spill, said study lead author Tracey Sutton, a biological oceanographer at Nova Southeastern University. A 2011 post-spill exploration cited in the research, which used six sets of nets at different depths and acoustic sonar, gave scientists a good sense of how much sea life was in the area between the surface and 5,000 feet deep. They returned to the same place with the same equipment three-and-a-half years later and found sea life was between one-third and one-quarter of what it was in 2011. “We saw this big decline,” Sutton said. “The question was then why? So we looked at all of the natural variables we thought could account for it, namely temperature, oxygen supply and food. None of those vary with the decline. The event that did was the oil spill. So we think that’s the most likely cause of the decline.” Researchers kept on sampling since 2015 and the low populations remained, with a slight rise in 2022 and 2023 that did not prove statistically significant or lasting, Sutton said. Documenting the decline Sutton's team documented the population declines with three different lines of evidence: what they caught in the nets, what their acoustic sonar found and genetic studies showing the species losing genetic diversity because of inbreeding. A lot of marine life died instantly after the explosion, which killed 11 workers, and from nearly five months of leaking oil and gas. Those pollutants got stored in the eggs of survivors and subsequent generations of critters got more compromised and weaker, Sutton said. BP spokesperson Paul Takahashi said the accident “forever changed” the company: “We have made many changes intended to help prevent an event like this from ever happening again.” Both the oil and the dispersants used to clean the spill hurt fish, but in different ways, said study co-author Isabel Romero, a chemical oceanographer at the University of South Carolina. Oil is more toxic and an overall threat, but the dispersant breaks the oil into smaller droplets, increasing the exposure of animals that live in the deeper water column, she said. Dispersants caused many problems, and new studies show that in future accidents, it would be better to avoid those chemicals and instead add agents that increase oil-munching microbes, said former National Science Foundation Director Rita Colwell, a University of Maryland environmental microbiologist who headed a 10-year, $500 million BP-funded program to study spill effects. Sutton said his team couldn’t prove an exact causal link to the BP oil spill, but by eliminating the other possibilities and looking at the timing, it’s logically clear that the spill caused the problem. The krill population dropped 72%. Lanternfish — odd fish with blue-green lights embedded over their bodies — are a third of what they used to be, Sutton said. The stunning but scary dragonfish — with sharp teeth, light organs and a lure attached to its head — also had big losses, he said. “These are foundational species,” Sutton said. “They're the things most things eat. So it's no wonder that we had wholesale changes across the community.” The inner ocean is more unknown than outer space Scientists learned much about this unexplored area of the Gulf. “One of our biggest findings from the whole thing is how connected the whole oceanic Gulf is from top to bottom because the animals move up and down,” Sutton said. “There are predators at the top that dive deep. Lots of things that are deep that come up at night. So the system is one very large pulsing system, rather than just a layered system like people might have thought beforehand.” Outside scientists were especially bothered by where the spill damaged. “We know more about space in some ways than we do about the inner ocean. Because we can’t see these regions, there is a tendency to assume everything is fine, but here we have a clear result showing that something went very wrong," Scripps Institution of Oceanography marine scientist Kaitlin Frasier said in an email. Frasier, who wasn't part of the study released Monday, published a post-spill study in 2024 looking at Gulf of Mexico whales and dolphins, finding population drops as high as 83%. “It’s shocking how a single failure in a drilling rig can have this vast and sustained impact over thousands of square kilometers, with little visible recovery over 13 years after the spill,” said Dalhousie University marine scientist Boris Worm, who wasn't part of the study. “It is important that we see this, because for the longest time these consequences were completely out of sight and out of mind.” Worm and Colwell said this damage should be kept in mind as the world talks about deep-sea mining and increased oil drilling in deep waters.

articles.title: Elon Musk’s proposed SpaceX stock giveaway would go into ‘Trump Accounts’
articles.summary: President Donald Trump announced this afternoon that Elon Musk’s promised SpaceX stock for children, which Musk revealed today, will be given through Trump Accounts.
articles.body: President Donald Trump announced this afternoon that Elon Musk’s SpaceX shares for children will be given through Trump Accounts. Musk said earlier today that he would give one of his SpaceX shares to “every kid in America” sometime next year. Musk had thanked Trump Account booster Brad Gerstner for “helping enable this,” and Trump appeared to confirm the plan in a post on Truth Social. Given the value of SpaceX’s stock on Friday, 72 million shares would be worth approximately $10.5 billion, according to CNBC. “This will be the first of many,” Musk said. Michael and Susan Dell, Ray and Barbara Dalio, Gerstner, and SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell have all also promised contributions to Trump Accounts. In October, the White House said that after automatically enrolling some 60 million children, over 70 million accounts had been created.

articles.title: After Dario Amodei’s donation, Elon Musk makes a promise to every kid in America: ‘I will give …’
articles.summary: Elon Musk, the world’s richest man has announced to give every American kid a slice of his SpaceX shares.
articles.body: Elon Musk, the world’s richest man has announced to give every American kid a slice of his SpaceX shares. “Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many,” the tech billionaire wrote on X (formerly Twitter). Musk’s post comes after Claude-maker Anthropic announced to donate a portion of the company’s shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new wholly owned entity dedicated entirely to the public benefit. The company led by Dario Amodei said that for every 50% increase in the company’s value over a set baseline, it will contribute up to an extra 2%.Elon Musk’s net worthElon Musk has an estimated net worth of $904 billion. As per the SEC filing in August, he owns about 4.8 billion SpaceX shares. When considering his unvested awards and stock options, the number rises to 6.4 billion.It is estimated that America’s roughly 72 million children under the age of 18 would each get one share currently worth $146.03, per SpaceX’s closing stock price on October 19. This totals to a whopping $10.5 billion worth of the aerospace company’s stock.Elon Musk’s donation to kids comes after Anthropic committed 5% of its shares to fundAs mentioned above, Musk’s donation to kids in America comes hours after Anthropic announced plans to commit 5% of its shares to a new “public benefit” fund. The Tesla founder responded to Anthropic’s announcement on X, writing: “I recommend giving the shares directly to the public.”“This is what I will be doing,” he said in another post then.Elon Musk has previously predicted that AI will lead to the era of abundance, where tech will do most of the work, thereby reducing the need for people to earn a living. He has also talked about universal basic income.“My prediction is that there will be effectively universal high income,” Musk said in an interview last month with state-owned China Media Group. “In fact, it’s not clear to me that money will even matter in the future.”“Universal HIGH INCOME via checks issued by the Federal government is the best way to deal with unemployment caused by AI,” Elon Musk posted to X in April this year.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: El misterio de la sustancia blanca de las momias chinas: un queso tipo kéfir de hace 3.600 años
articles.standfirst: El ADN resuelve un enigma de más de veinte años
articles.summary: El ADN resuelve un enigma de más de veinte años
articles.body: Durante más de dos décadas, unos misteriosos restos blancos esparcidos sobre varias momias chinas desconcertaron a los arqueólogos. Hoy se sabe que no eran un ungüento ni un ritual funerario desconocido, sino algo mucho más cotidiano: queso. En concreto, un queso de kéfir de unos 3.600 años de antigüedad, el más antiguo del que se conserva una muestra. Las momias fueron halladas en el cementerio de Xiaohe, en la cuenca del Tarim, en el noroeste de China. Datan de la Edad del Bronce, de hace entre 3.300 y 3.600 años, y el clima seco de la región las ha conservado en un estado excepcional. La sustancia aparecía sobre la cabeza y el cuello de varios cuerpos, entre ellos el de una mujer enterrada con sombrero de fieltro, abrigo de lana y botas forradas de piel. El misterio se resolvió gracias a los avances en el análisis de ADN antiguo. Un equipo de la Academia China de Ciencias, dirigido por la paleogenetista Qiaomei Fu, extrajo material genético de muestras de tres tumbas distintas. Los resultados, publicados en la revista Cell, revelaron ADN de vaca y de cabra, y microorganismos presentes en los actuales granos de kéfir, como la bacteria Lactobacillus kefiranofaciens y la levadura Pichia kudriavzevii. El kéfir se elabora fermentando la leche con granos que contienen bacterias y levaduras, de forma parecida a la masa madre del pan. Para los investigadores, este proceso pudo ser clave para un pueblo genéticamente intolerante a la lactosa, ya que la fermentación reduce su contenido y alarga la conservación de la leche. El estudio sugiere que en Xiaohe usaban leche de vaca y de cabra por separado, a diferencia de otras tradiciones queseras, como las de Grecia u Oriente Próximo, que las mezclaban. Pero el gran valor del hallazgo está en la posibilidad de comparar las bacterias antiguas con las actuales. “Es un estudio sin precedentes, que nos permite observar cómo ha evolucionado una bacteria durante los últimos 3.000 años”, explicó Fu.
